sources.claim: Provider rule of thumb (OpenAI help article): for English text one token is about 4 characters or about three quarters of a word; exact counts depend on the model and its tokenizer. Token counts are not word counts.

sections.skill: Estimate a metered cost from token counts and rates

questions.prompt: What is a token?

choices.text: A chunk of text a model reads or writes
A coin that you must buy from the provider

questions.correct_answer: A chunk of text a model reads or writes
questions.intro: Metered AI pricing is often based on TOKENS: chunks of text that models read and write. As a provider rule of thumb for English, one token is about 4 characters or about three-quarters of a word, but exact counts depend on the model. Many services charge separately for INPUT tokens (what you send) and OUTPUT tokens (what the model writes), often at different rates, quoted per million tokens. To estimate a cost: divide each token count by 1,000,000, multiply by its rate, and add the two results.

sections.skill: Compute a per-million cost in three steps

questions.prompt: 2,000,000 tokens is how many millions?

choices.text: 20, because you count the number of zeros in the number and divide that by three

questions.intro: To price tokens quoted "per million": (1) DIVIDE the token count by 1,000,000 to get millions. (2) MULTIPLY by the rate. (3) ADD input and output costs. Example with hypothetical rates of 3 dollars per million input and 12 per million output: 2,000,000 input tokens is 2 million x 3 = 6 dollars; 250,000 output tokens is 0.25 million x 12 = 3 dollars; total 9 dollars.

questions.prompt: 250,000 tokens is how many millions?

choices.text: 25, since there are two hundred and fifty thousand tokens, which rounds to twenty-five

questions.prompt: Why do long conversations cost more per message over time?
questions.intro: Estimates go wrong in predictable ways. In many metered products a long conversation resends earlier messages as input, so processed input grows, though some products trim, summarize or discount repeated text. Attached documents add the text actually processed. Output is often priced higher, so for the same input, longer answers cost more. Some languages use more tokens for the same meaning. Before running a big job, test a small sample, measure the actual tokens used, and then multiply.
